extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law students, scholars of Hobbes
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition (from Hobbes' Leviathan) setting out criteria and principles for understanding liberty, obligation, and the limits of sovereign and subordinate political bodies. It provides definitions, case-based rules, and examples for when subjects retain or lose liberties and when representatives act for a body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined as absence of external impediment
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty (properly) is not an ability of the will or voice but the absence of external stop or impediment to action; e.g., 'the way is free' means those who walk in it are not stopped; a gift is called free of the giver who was not bound; 'speak freely' means no law obliged the speaker otherwise; 'freewill' refers to liberty of the man, not of appetite or inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that 'free' refers to absence of restraint on the person: walking without stop, a giver not bound by covenant, a speaker not law-obliged. Emphasize liberty as negative (no external impediment) rather than metaphysical freedom of desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear and liberty are consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done from fear can still be acts of a free person; fear does not necessarily remove voluntariness — e.g., throwing goods into the sea to save a ship or paying a debt for fear of imprisonment are actions of one at liberty because they could refuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between being compelled by physical restraint and acting under fear of consequences; fear can produce willing action so long as no external physical impediment prevents refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty and necessity are consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions proceed from the will (liberty) yet also have causal antecedents (necessity); every act of will has causes in a chain ultimately rooted in God, so liberty of action coexists with a necessary causal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy of water descending a channel: actions can be freely willed and yet necessary in a causal chain. This resolves apparent contradiction between human liberty and divine omnipotence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial bonds or covenants create civil laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealths (the artificial man) create 'artificial chains' (civil laws) by mutual covenants fastening powers to a sovereign and to subjects' ears; these bonds are weak in nature but held by danger rather than by difficulty of breaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil laws derive authority from covenants among subjects and delegation to a sovereign. The force maintaining these bonds is the danger of breaking them (punishment), not metaphysical inviolability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of subjects consists in liberty from covenants (praetermitted acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a commonwealth cannot regulate all actions, subjects retain liberty in actions the sovereign has praetermitted (left undetermined by law): e.g., buying, selling, choosing abode, diet, trade, instituting children, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify that subject liberty is limited to what the sovereign has not commanded; liberty does not imply exemption from all law nor a right to endanger others' lives or the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject liberty compatible with sovereign's unlimited power
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject liberty does not abolish or limit the sovereign's power of life and death; actions of the sovereign cannot properly be called injustice to subjects because subjects are authors of sovereign acts via their consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scriptural and historical examples (Jeptha, David, Athens' ostracism) to show that sovereign acts—even those leading to a subject's death—are not injustice to the subject in civil terms, though may be sin against God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty lauded by classical writers is liberty of commonwealths, not private men
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient praise of 'liberty' (Greeks/Romans) refers to the freedom of states (commonwealths) to act, not individual freedoms; conflating the two produces error and may fuel sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: importing Athenian/Roman notions of liberty into other constitutional contexts can mislead subjects into demanding private rights that undermine sovereign authority and public peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to measure the liberty of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty of the subject is inferred from what rights are passed away in making a commonwealth, derived either from explicit words of submission ('I authorise all his actions') or from the intention of submission (end: peace and defense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine obligations and retained liberties by examining the explicit terms of submission or the purpose for which sovereignty was established (peace and protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects retain liberty to defend their own bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants that require a man not to defend his own body are void; subjects keep liberty in matters whose right cannot be transferred by covenant (self-preservation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to earlier treatment (chapter 14): natural right of self-defense persists; sovereign commands cannot morally/contractually bind a person to forego necessary self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects are not bound to hurt themselves or self-incriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: If sovereign commands a condemned man to wound or kill himself, or to abstain from essentials without which he cannot live, the man has liberty to disobey; likewise a subject is not bound to confess a crime without assurance of pardon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent phrases like 'I authorise all his actions' do not imply consent to self-harm; obligations depend on intention and the ends of submission—disobedience is allowed where obedience would require impossible self-injury or self-accusation without pardon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects not obliged to warfare unless voluntarily undertaken
rubrics_metrics.description: A man commanded as a soldier may often refuse to fight (without injustice) unless he voluntarily enlisted, substituted another, or took impress money; cowardice is dishonorable but not always unjust; when full defense of the commonwealth requires all able-bodied assistance, obligation may be absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowances for natural timorousness; substitution is acceptable if it preserves the commonwealth's service; voluntary undertakings (enrollment, pay) remove excuses; when universal defense is necessary, individual refusal undermines the covenant and may be punishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liberty to resist the sovereign's sword to defend another
rubrics_metrics.description: One may not resist the sovereign's authority in defense of another (guilty or innocent) because such resistance withdraws sovereign means of protection and threatens the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if many have already resisted unjustly, subsequent resistance in self-defense may not be unjust; offer of pardon removes the plea of self-defense and makes continued resistance unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest liberty of subjects depends on the law's silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the sovereign's law prescribes nothing, the subject has liberty to act according to private discretion; thus liberties vary by place and time depending on what the sovereign has chosen to regulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: forcible entry previously allowed but later abolished by statute; polygamy allowed in some places and not in others. On legal disputes with sovereign based on a prior law, subjects may sue like any other litigant; but where sovereign acts by prerogative (power), ordinary remedy may be absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants of liberty contrary to sovereign safety are void
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sovereign grants liberty that incapacitates his ability to provide for subjects' safety (e.g., power necessary for war, judicature, levying money), the grant is void unless he renounces or transfers sovereignty explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret purported grants in light of sovereign's continued intention; consequences inconsistent with retained sovereign powers indicate the grant was not intended or is void for repugnancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience lasts only while sovereign can protect
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects' obligation to the sovereign endures as long as the sovereign's power to protect continues; natural right to self-protection cannot be extinguished by covenant, and the commonwealth's soul (sovereignty) can die by war or internal discord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When protection evaporates (e.g., conquest, collapse), subjects ethically may revert to natural liberty; the end (protection) is the measuring stick of valid obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for captivity and acceptance of victor's sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subject is taken prisoner and accepts conditions to be subject to the victor to preserve life, he thereby becomes subject to the victor; if detained without loss of bodily liberty, such submission is not implied and escape is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary acceptance of conditions for preservation of life yields legitimate subjecthood to the victor; coercive detention without consensual acceptance does not bind by covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: If sovereign relinquishes government, subjects return to natural liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a monarch relinquishes sovereignty for himself and heirs (or dies without heir), subjects return to absolute liberty of nature because there is no recognized sovereign to whom to submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a declared heir or explicit renunciation dissolves institutional subjection; natural rules of kinship do not suffice to recreate sovereignty without the monarch's will or appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banishment and temporary absence from dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: A banished subject is not subject during banishment; one sent on message or traveling with leave remains subject (by contract between sovereigns, not by covenant of subjection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between exile (loss of subjection during banishment) and temporary absence with leave (continued subject status under inter-sovereign contract or license).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect when sovereign becomes subject to another
rubrics_metrics.description: If a monarch is subdued and becomes subject to a victor, his subjects become obliged to the victor; if the monarch is merely a prisoner without liberty, his sovereign right remains and previous magistrates may continue administration in his name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between voluntary submission (which transfers subjects' obligations) and coercive captivity (which may leave original sovereign rights intact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and taxonomy of 'Systemes' (political bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: SYSTEMES are numbers of men joined in one interest or business; they can be regular (one man or assembly represents whole) or irregular (mere concourse). Regular can be absolute/independent (commonwealths) or dependent/subordinate; private vs political; lawful vs unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification matters for rights and liabilities: bodies politic created by sovereign authority differ from private associations; large concourses may be lawful if harmless but unlawful if intentions are evil or numbers are considerable and unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: In bodies politique the representative's power is limited by sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The representative's power is always limited; the sovereign prescribes the limits, and only by express grant (letters) or law may a representative act beyond ordinary bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlimited representative power equals absolute sovereignty; to avoid dividing dominion, sovereigns ordinarily limit subordinate representatives by letters patents and by the common laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters patents as limits on representative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In subordinate bodies, diverse limitations concerning business, times, and places must be set out in writing (letters patent) sealed or testified so they can be read and relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a body's authority is locale- or task-specific, permanent written evidence of the scope of powers is necessary for clarity and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary laws determine representative actions where letters are silent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where letters patents are silent, the ordinary common laws of the commonwealth determine what a representative may lawfully do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the common law as fallback limits; absence of written grant does not imply limitless authority for subordinate bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: When representative is one man, unwarranted acts are his alone
rubrics_metrics.description: If the representative is a single person, acts beyond his letters or the laws are his own acts, not acts of the body or its members; acts within letters/laws are acts of everyone represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit & liability rest on the scope of delegated authority; outsiders dealing with a representative should inspect letters to know who's bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: When representative is an assembly, only assenters are bound by unwarranted decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: In an assembly, decrees not warranted by letters or law are the act of the assembly and those who voted for them; they are not the act of those who voted against or were absent (unless by proxy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissenters recorded their votes or protests to avoid collective liability; punishments for assemblies may include dissolution or forfeiture of letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability rules for debts contracted by representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If the representative is one man who borrows from outsiders, the debt is his alone; when an assembly borrows, only those who assented are responsible; if a debt is to a member of the assembly, the body (common stock) is liable, not individual members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish creditor type (stranger vs assembly member) and the form of representation (single vs assembly) when assessing who is legally bound to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protestations against decrees lawful in subordinate bodies but not against sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes lawful and expedient for a subject to protest and register dissent against decrees of subordinate representative assemblies to avoid becoming responsible; protesting against sovereign decrees denies sovereignty and is not lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recorded protest to protect personal liability in subordinate bodies; never expect to lawfully protest sovereign commands without challenging the foundation of subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodies politique governing provinces/colonies have strictly limited jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies governing provinces, colonies, towns, universities, or corporations have powers limited by commission and cannot execute authority outside their territorial bounds (e.g., seize property outside the colony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions beyond jurisdiction are invalid; remedies for members injured by the body belong to the sovereign's courts, not the body itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies for trade create monopolies beneficial to merchants but harmful to public
rubrics_metrics.description: In bodies politic for foreign traffic, incorporation grants a 'double monopoly' (sole buyers at home and sole sellers abroad), which increases merchants' gains but disadvantages people at home (higher prices) and foreigners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn that trade corporations' institutional monopoly privileges serve merchant profit but can be detrimental to the general populace's welfare.
